kakekotoba.reading_primary: そよ(interjection: そのとおり/well then)
kakekotoba.reading_secondary: そよ(onomatopoeia: rustling sound of wind)
kakekotoba.interaction: そよ echoes the rustling sound the wind makes in the bamboo grass (an onomatopoeic mimicry of 'sayo-sayo' wind-in-leaves) while simultaneously functioning as the exclamatory 'that's it!' / 'indeed' interjection introducing the speaker's assertion in the shimo-no-ku — the sound of the wind in the sasawara is literally re-heard in the word that pivots the poem into direct address.

jokotoba.text: ありま山猪名の笹原風吹けば
jokotoba.function: The entire kami-no-ku (place names Arima-yama and Ina no Sasawara, plus the image of wind blowing through the bamboo grass) is a freely-composed extended preface that leads, through the sound 'そよ' (the rustling of the grass), into the shimo-no-ku's exclamation 'いでそよ' — it establishes both a real landscape and an auditory bridge into the poem's emotional statement, rather than being a fixed epithet.

honkadori.source_poem: Attributed in some sources to an anonymous poem in the Shinkokinshu/earlier tradition referencing Arima-yama and Ina no Sasawara wind imagery
honkadori.echoed_phrase: ありま山ゐなの笹原風吹けば
honkadori.function: Daini no Sanmi draws on a traditional place-name pairing (Arima-yama / Ina no Sasawara) already associated with the imagery of wind stirring bamboo grass, lending her poem an air of established poetic diction even as she turns it toward a personal reproach to a fickle lover — though the precise ur-source poem is not securely attested, the phrase carries the flavor of quotation from established utamakura tradition.

kigo.note: The wind blowing through the sasawara (bamboo grass) is not tied to a specific season in this poem; it functions primarily as an auditory device generating the pivot 'そよ' rather than as a seasonal marker. Other candidate images — 笹原 (bamboo grass, evergreen, non-seasonal), ありま山/猪名 (place names, non-seasonal) — likewise carry no strong seasonal charge. This poem is essentially a-seasonal, a love poem (relationship/reproach poem) built on landscape and sound rather than seasonal observation, so season is best marked as none despite the presence of a wind image.

bipartite.kami_theme: A landscape of Mount Arima and the bamboo grass of Ina, stirred and made to rustle audibly when the wind blows — a scene of natural motion and sound.
bipartite.shimo_theme: The speaker turns sharply to address her lover directly: 'That's it — how could I ever forget you?' asserting through rhetorical question that her feelings, unlike the shifting wind, remain constant.
bipartite.pivot_note: The kami-no-ku is not merely scenic backdrop but a jokotoba whose culminating sound (そよ, the rustle of wind in grass) is reused as the very interjection that launches the shimo-no-ku's passionate rhetorical question; the natural image of wind that comes and goes ironically underscores the shimo's claim of steadfast, unwavering love, producing a poem that pivots from auditory landscape to emotional avowal through wordplay rather than through simple causation or simile.
